title: Relocation threats and what followed

rows.owners: Marv Wolfenson & Harvey Ratner (sellers); Glen Taylor (buyer, Aug 1994, $88.5M)
rows.said_or_done: Paraphrase (Wikipedia citing Star Tribune 1994-02-12): owners sought a public or private buyer for the $73M remaining Target Center mortgage, otherwise the team "would be sold and in all likelihood moved"; owners met San Diego, Nashville and New Orleans representatives (Feb 1994). 1994-05-23: agreed to sell to Top Rank of Louisiana for $152.5M to move to New Orleans (Times-Picayune 1994-05-24).
rows.league_role: opposed: Stern mediated (1994-02-11); relocation committee unanimously blocked sale 1994-06-15; NBA sued to enjoin transfer
rows.money_after: Public purchase of Target Center: Laws of Minnesota 1994 ch. 648 (HF 3041) signed 1994-05-10; reported purchase price $48M (Star Tribune via Wikipedia); Minneapolis final financing approval Mar 1995
rows.mechanism: Metropolitan Sports Facilities Commission/City purchase financed by bonds (ticket-surcharge backed; 1995 revised plan incl. $12.7M business bond commitments)
rows.vote: Legislature + City Council; no referendum (poll: 60% opposed intervention)
rows.label: b (LRL, OLA 2017) + c
rows.notes: Purchase price $54.6M (b, Minnesota Legislative Auditor 2017: "Minneapolis spent an additional $54.6 million to purchase the facility"), the funding ledger's figure; $48M (Star Tribune via Wikipedia, c) is the alternative. Threat dated from the LRL timeline: "1994 January: Reports surface that Wolfenson and Ratner are considering moving the team to San Diego or Nashville" (day not given; 15th used); Stern mediated Feb 11. Final city approval Mar 23 1995 (Star Tribune headline, "As of Today, Target Center Financing is a Done Deal", via LRL).

rows.said_or_done: No relocation threat documented; Ackerley had floated a private SoDo arena; city offered Coliseum renovation instead.
rows.money_after: Seattle Center Coliseum -> KeyArena renovation: city $74.5M (Sonics ~$21M); council 7-2 (May 1993), 15-yr lease
rows.mechanism: City bonds repaid from arena revenue sharing
rows.label: c
rows.notes: Comparison group N.

rows.said_or_done: Verbatim (Miami New Times, 1996-11-14): "Back in June the shipping magnate forced the county into an agreement by threatening to move to Broward, a tactic his own negotiators later admitted was a bluff." Arison also sued (unsuccessfully) to block the ballot initiative, then funded an ad campaign.
rows.money_after: Miami-Dade: $38M bayfront county land + county operating payments ($8.5M/yr in the deal announced days before the vote; later reported $6.4M/yr; $64M paid by 2010); county gets 40% of arena profits above $14M (paid once, $257,134 in 2013; deleted in the 2014 amended agreements)
rows.mechanism: Land + annual operating subsidy from county; Heat financed the $213M building
rows.label: c
rows.notes: First approval Mar 29 1996: emergency meetings of the Dade County and Miami city commissions approved a $210M plan and a letter of intent was signed the same day (Miami New Times, May 8 1996, which also dates the Broward threat to early 1996, an anecdote of Feb 23 1996); the Inspector General (IG11-34) calls that letter of intent non-binding; county deal for a $165M arena in June 1996; referendum Nov 5 1996; binding agreements April 1997. FY2025-26 county budget still shows a $6.4M payment.

rows.said_or_done: Council weighed a $70M loan to keep the Kings in town (SportsBusiness Daily headline 1997-01-31); later accounts say Thomas threatened to sell the money-losing team (secondary).
rows.money_after: City loan to team ~$70M (1997); balance reported as $77M owed to the city in 2011
rows.label: u (weak documentation of threat; loan amount reported inconsistently $70M-$82M)
rows.notes: Not counted as a threat (reclassified Oct 18 2026): the record shows only a council loan "to keep the Kings in town" (SBD headline) and later secondary accounts that Thomas threatened to sell; no other city, out clause, out-of-town buyer or offer without a limit on moving is documented, and statements by officials alone do not count. Excluded from the capital comparison (loan).

rows.said_or_done: No Mavericks owner statement found. Days before the vote, David Deniger, CEO of Hicks's Olympus Realty, a Stars minority owner and an arena negotiator, said "It's not unreasonable to assume the teams are going to go elsewhere" if the vote failed, with an arena near the Ballpark in Arlington, adding "we haven't threatened anybody" (Dallas Observer, Jan 14 1998). Owners supplied >$1.6M of the >$1.9M pro-arena campaign (backers outspent opponents ~20:1).
rows.money_after: $125M city contribution to $420M American Airlines Center (+>$60M infrastructure; $185.3M public through 2018 per city)
rows.label: c
rows.notes: Treated as no documented threat (N) with an "unclear" flag; sensitivity drops it. The Deniger statement (added Oct 18 2026) came from a minority owner of the co-tenant NHL team, not the Mavericks, and disclaimed a threat, so it is recorded but not counted.

rows.said_or_done: No specific 1998-99 owner threat found in this pass. Peter J. Holt (2022 letter): "My family became involved in the Spurs in the 90s because there was a real threat the team would be moved."
rows.money_after: SBC (now Frost Bank) Center $175M: Bexar County bonds backed by hotel-occupancy and car-rental tax increases; Spurs $28.5M (public $146.5M, 84%)
rows.label: c
rows.notes: Treated as N with "unclear" flag.

rows.said_or_done: After voters rejected the arena (Nov 1999), Commissioner David Stern: "if there's not a new building...I think it's certain that the team will be relocated." (Houston Chronicle, 2000-02-13). Rockets talked to other cities: looked at Anaheim in 1999-2000 (LA Times 2001-02-13) and negotiated with Louisville ("Louisville Woos Rockets", Houston Chronicle 2000-05-13).
rows.money_after: Toyota Center: city/Harris County-Houston Sports Authority $182M of $235M (77%); Rockets $43M; city bought land
rows.mechanism: Harris County-Houston Sports Authority financing; campaign promised "no new taxes of any kind"
rows.vote: City Council ~2000-09-13; voters 2000-11-07, 66% yes (1999 version had failed). Pro campaign: Enron/Ken Lay $590K, Reliant $400K
rows.label: c
rows.notes: Stern quote via Wikipedia citation of the Chronicle (archive not fetched).

rows.said_or_done: 2001-03-26: Hornets applied to relocate to Memphis (SI/CNN 2001-03-26); withdrew when arena was put in a non-binding referendum; referendum failed June 2001 (43% yes / 57% no). City leaders then said they would not build unless Shinn sold; Hornets requested a move to New Orleans.
rows.league_role: backed relocation (NBA approved move 2002-05-10) and promised Charlotte an expansion team if an arena deal was reached
rows.money_after: Same owner/city: none. After departure: Charlotte City Council 2002-11-11 (8-3, no referendum) approved ~$260-265M arena for the expansion Bobcats. Destination: Louisiana 10-yr lease at state-owned New Orleans Arena ($114M, opened 1999) + practice facility (state pledged $6.5M) + inducements (not itemized)
rows.mechanism: Charlotte: city-financed arena, no referendum; local companies to put up $50M, recouped via city land incl. the old Coliseum site (ESPN 2002)
rows.label: c
rows.notes: Money followed actual departure, for a new league-awarded team (league-conditioned).

rows.owners: Michael Heisley (bought 2001-01-25 for $160M); earlier buyer Bill Laurie (1999-2000)
rows.said_or_done: Heisley said at purchase he would keep the team in Vancouver (Chicago Tribune 2001-01-25), then sought relocation; NBA allowed him to explore a move (ABC News 2001-02-12); applied to move to Memphis 2001-03-26. Laurie's 1999 deal carried a $52M bonus if the team moved to St. Louis; NBA opposed.
rows.alt_city: Memphis, Louisville, Anaheim, New Orleans, Las Vegas, Nashville, Tampa, Buffalo, San Diego (St. Louis in 1999)
rows.league_role: Stern opposed relocation in 1999; Board approved Memphis move unanimously 2001-07-03
rows.money_after: Destination: Memphis/Shelby County $250M FedExForum (Public Building Authority bonds; sales-tax rebates, hotel and car-rental taxes) = 100% public. Offers: Louisville $200M arena (+Tricon $5M/yr x20); Las Vegas free land. Vancouver: no public offer found
rows.vote: City/County approval 2001 (date not verified); no referendum
rows.label: c
rows.notes: Approval date = NBA approval (local approval preceded it); lag is an upper bound.

rows.said_or_done: AP via ESPN 2002-01-12: "Magic owner Rich DeVos plans to sell the team and won't require the new owners to keep it in Orlando." DeVos: "I can't ask him to do anything" but "I don't see any reason why he would want to leave Orlando." Team claimed ~$10M/yr losses blamed on arena.
rows.alt_city: none named by owner (NY Sun later described Kansas City as leverage)
rows.league_role: neutral (Vander Weide met Stern about finding a partner)
rows.money_after: Amway (now Kia) Center $480M ($380M arena + $100M land/infrastructure): Magic >= $50M upfront + overruns + $1M/yr rent x30; rest public via Orange County tourist-development-tax bonds and city land (~90% public per PFM)
rows.mechanism: Tourist development (hotel) tax bonds; city land/infrastructure
rows.vote: Orlando council 6-1 (2007-07-23); Orange County 5-2 (2007-07-26); final 2007-08-06; no referendum
rows.label: c
rows.notes: Long lag (66 months) - excluded under a 36-month-window sensitivity.

rows.said_or_done: Jan 2006 (Pollstar 2006-01-31): Shinn said New Orleans was not ready and argued the team should stay in Oklahoma City, asking "What if next October there's 10 feet of water in the city?"
rows.league_role: team returned for 2007-08 (league position not verified here)
rows.money_after: No new public package identified in this pass; returned under the 2002 lease
rows.label: c (quote via search summary of Pollstar; not fetched)
rows.notes: Counts as threat without new money.

rows.said_or_done: "Allen's Trail Blazers Seek Help to Stay in Portland" (Seattle Times 2006-02-25); team put up for sale June 2006 (Oregonian 2006-06-07), later taken off the market; "much speculation that the Trail Blazers might leave".
rows.money_after: None identified; Allen privately re-bought the Rose Garden from creditors in 2007
rows.label: c
rows.notes: Counts as threat without new money.

rows.owners: Howard Schultz (sold 2006-07-18) -> Clay Bennett, Aubrey McClendon, Tom Ward et al. (PBC)
rows.said_or_done: Schultz sold to the Oklahoma City group after failing to get $220M for KeyArena (2006). 2007-08-13: McClendon told The Journal Record the group bought the team intending to move it to Oklahoma City (NBA fined him $250,000; Seattle Times 2007-08-23). 2007-11-02: Bennett told Stern the team would move to Oklahoma City (ESPN 2007-11-03).
rows.alt_city: Oklahoma City (Renton, WA arena also proposed)
rows.money_after: Seattle: none (Initiative 91, Nov 2006, 74% yes, restricted subsidies; state/local governments did not fund a $500M arena complex). Destination: Oklahoma City voters 2008-03-04 approved 15-month 1-cent sales tax for $121.6M Ford Center upgrades + practice facility (62%); collected $103.5M. Seattle got $45M lease-break settlement (2008-07-02)
rows.label: c
rows.notes: Lag measured to destination-city money. Oklahoma also made sports teams eligible for 15-year Quality Jobs payroll rebates (SB 1819, approved with an emergency clause Apr 17 2008, the day before the NBA vote; b, https://www.oklegislature.gov/BillInfo.aspx?Bill=SB1819&Session=0800); the Tax Commission paid the team $14.87M in FY2010-FY2013 (b, Quality Jobs Incentive Payment Reports via Digital Prairie), and a 2023 law (SB 604) extended sports-team contracts to 30 years. Not counted in the funding ledger (a memo, like the Pelicans' pre-lease rebates).

rows.said_or_done: Bond Buyer 2010-07-13: "The team has said for more than two years that it cannot afford the $18 million annual cost of running the fieldhouse." IBJ 2010-07-16: lease runs to 2019 "but the team has the right to opt out"; board member David Shane raised the possibility Simon might sell.
rows.money_after: Capital Improvement Board 2010-07-16 (6-1): $33.5M over 3 years ($10M/yr operating + >=$3.5M capital); partial repayment if team leaves before 2019
rows.label: c
rows.notes: Threat start approximated from "more than two years" (mid-2008). Operating money: excluded from capital comparison.

rows.said_or_done: Lease let the team leave if two-year average attendance fell below a benchmark (reported 14,735; another report 14,883); league ran the team while seeking a local owner. Stern called the March 2012 lease "an important and necessary step toward reaching an agreement with a new owner."
rows.money_after: 2012-03-16 Gov. Jindal announced 10-yr extension to 2024 with ~$50M state-funded arena upgrades (bond issue needing legislative approval); exit clause removed. LSED audits show "revenue benchmark" inducement payments continued ($2.59M FY2014; $2.84M FY2023) plus players' income-tax pass-through (~$2.1-2.6M/yr)
rows.label: c + b (LLA audits)
rows.notes: Governor's office said inducements would end; audits show benchmark payments continued under the restated agreement.

rows.said_or_done: 2011-02-19: Stern acknowledged Kings-Anaheim relocation talks; team filed trademark "Anaheim Royals" (NBA.com 2011-03-16). Anaheim council (2011-03-29, unanimous) approved $75M bonds ($25M Honda Center upgrades, $50M working capital) to Henry Samueli's companies.
rows.league_role: no approval sought to completion: Maloofs withdrew the bid (April 2011) after Sacramento pledged support; Stern had acknowledged the talks
rows.money_after: Sacramento council 2012-03-06 approved term sheet: city $255.5M of $391M arena; Maloofs backed out 2012-04-13 (not executed)
rows.label: c
rows.notes: Not executed - excluded from money comparison.

rows.owners: Maloofs -> sale agreement with Chris Hansen & Steve Ballmer group (2013-01-21) -> Vivek Ranadive group (2013-05)
rows.said_or_done: 2013-01-21: Maloofs agreed to sell 65% at a $525M valuation to the Seattle group, which was expected to relocate and use the SuperSonics name (USA Today 2013-01-21); relocation application filed (ESPN 2013-02-06); bid raised to $625M valuation (2013-05-10).
rows.alt_city: Seattle (SoDo arena MOU: up to $200M public, approved 2012-09-24 city 6-2 / 2012-10-15 county)
rows.league_role: opposed the move: relocation committee 7-0 against (2013-04-29); Board rejected relocation 22-8 (2013-05-15); the NBA also told the city it must open the arena by 2017 or risk losing the Kings (AP, 2014)
rows.money_after: Golden 1 Center: council approved public financing 2014-05-20; city ~$223M cash ($212M bonds + $11M parking/econ-dev funds) of $507M; commonly reported $255M incl. land
rows.mechanism: Lease-revenue bonds backed by parking revenue
rows.vote: City Council 2014-05-20; no public vote (petition drive opposed)
rows.label: c
rows.notes: Non-binding term sheet reported March 2013 (vote count not verified).

rows.owners: Herb Kohl -> Marc Lasry & Wes Edens (Apr 2014, $550M)
rows.said_or_done: Sale terms let the NBA "buy back the team for $575 million" if "construction on a new building in Milwaukee is not underway by the deadline" (BizTimes 2014-04-22, citing ESPN); Silver: league "prepared to insist that Milwaukee have a plan for a modern arena by 2017." 2015-07-06: Bucks president Peter Feigin told legislators the NBA could buy and move the team to "Las Vegas or Seattle" (KNPR 2015-07-07, citing Milwaukee Business Journal).
rows.money_after: 2015 Wisconsin Act 60: Wisconsin Center District $203M bonds (state GPR $4M/yr to 2035-36 + $4M/yr via cut to county aid; WCD tax revenue bonds) + City $47M TIF ($35M parking, $12M plaza) = $250M of $524.1M (47.7%)
rows.label: b (LFB) + c
rows.notes: Lag 15.7 months from the clause; 1.2 months from Feigin's warning.

rows.said_or_done: Arizona Republic (Laurie Roberts) reported Sarver told some council members he would move the team to Seattle or Las Vegas if no deal (HoopsRumors 2018-12-12). Disputed: Suns president Jason Rowley denied anyone in the organization threatened to leave (moving out of state a last resort); one council member backtracked; another reported Sarver said "just let me go somewhere else" (as reported; Republic said Sarver did not name the cities himself). Lease had a 2022 opt-out if the arena was deemed "obsolete".
rows.money_after: Council 2019-01-23 (6-2): city $150M (Sports Facilities Fund) of $230M renovation; Suns $80M; stay through 2037 (option to 2042); up to $200M penalty if they leave early
rows.label: c (threat reported, disputed)
rows.notes: Sensitivity drops it as disputed.

rows.said_or_done: Lease "Shortfall Season" clause (avg paid attendance < 14,900, 64 largest suites unsold, or < 2,500 club seats): city/county must buy the shortfall within 60 days or the team may terminate early (Commercial Appeal / Daily Memphian, June 2020).
rows.money_after: Shelby County Commission 2022-04-13 (unanimous): city+county pay $4.95M/yr for four seasons from 2021-22, then $6.3M/yr for four seasons (= $44.8M); team through 2029
rows.label: c
rows.notes: Operating money: excluded from capital comparison.

rows.said_or_done: Washington Post 2023-06-23: Monumental considering moving both teams to National Landing (Arlington) if DC did not invest. 2023-12-13: Leonsis and Gov. Glenn Youngkin announced a Potomac Yard (Alexandria) arena; plan relied on ~$1.05B project-revenue + $416M lease-revenue bonds, Monumental $403M, Alexandria $106M. House passed HB 1514 59-40; Senate Finance chair L. Louise Lucas refused to docket it; Alexandria declared the deal dead 2024-03-27.
rows.money_after: DC offered $500M (Dec 2023). 2024-03-27 deal: DC $515M (incl. ~$87.5M arena purchase), Monumental >= $285M; teams through 2050. Council unanimous emergency approval 2024-04-02; FY2025 budget 2024-06-12
rows.mechanism: DC capital budget over 3 years; arena bought and leased back
rows.label: c + b (D.C. Law 17-12)
rows.notes: 3.6 months from the explicit announcement; 9.3 months from the June 2023 report. In March 2024 the District's attorney general wrote that the teams were bound to play in Washington through 2047 under the 2007 bond deal (AP via NBC Washington, Mar 22 2024, c); D.C. Law 17-12 (2007) s.9(f)(4) required DC Arena to extend its ground lease by 20 years (b, https://code.dccouncil.gov/us/dc/council/laws/17-12). Monumental said a 2007 agreement let it prepay the bonds and revoke the extension on 120 days' notice (same AP story). The letter itself was not found.

rows.owners: Paul Allen estate (Jody Allen) -> Tom Dundon group (agreement 2025-08-13; NBA approval 2026-03-30; ~$4.25B)
rows.said_or_done: Sale to a Dallas-based buyer; the team was "not ... shy about dangling the possibility of Dundon moving the team" while lobbying the 2026 session (OPB, Apr 20 2026), and Dundon "has used the expansion process and the threat of relocation for leverage in recent discussions with other owners and city officials" (ESPN, Oct 2026); per OPB, Dundon's representatives "convinced state and local officials to finance renovations" before the purchase. KATU 2026-07-15: Dundon "has not publicly suggested he intends to move the franchise, but he also has not made a long-term commitment to keeping the team in Portland." Silver: "We are working with both sides to ensure that the Trail Blazers can have a long-term future in Portland." Oct 16 2026: Dundon called relocation "not a conversation" and said "we have four years to figure it out" before the lease ends (texts to The Athletic, via KGW). Oct 21 2026: "While the state's legislation requires a 20-year lease agreement," Dundon "has pushed for a buyout option after 10 years, multiple sources said"; in June 2026 he told the Portland Metro Chamber, "It feels like we're making a pretty big investment by staying here and paying these tax rates" (Oregonian).
rows.money_after: Oregon SB 1501 (passed early March 2026): state bonds up to $365M repaid from Rose Quarter income-tax withholding (incl. players), conditional on city/county commitments and a long-term lease; city/county ~$208M pending; council approved negotiating terms Aug 2026; council authorized the Joint Authority Agreement Oct 21 2026 (8-4) with no funding commitment (Ordinance 192244)
rows.mechanism: State bonds repaid by income-tax withholding at the arena
rows.label: c + b (enrolled bill, session law, ordinance)
rows.notes: SB 1501 passed the Senate Mar 4 and the House Mar 6 2026 (enrolled bill) and was signed Mar 31 2026 (Oregon Laws 2026, ch. 74). The money is approved but not final: definitive agreements and the bond sale are pending, so the comparison and the outcome counts treat it as pending, as the funding ledger does.

rows.said_or_done: Mayor David Holt (2022 State of the City): not funding a new arena could lead the Thunder to "look outside the state for a new home"; Holt (Nov 2023): without a yes vote "It will be the beginning of the end and there's no other real path" (PBS NewsHour 2023-11-15). No relocation statement by Bennett or the NBA found; Bennett: arena will "secure the long-term future of the Thunder."
rows.money_after: Voters 2023-12-12: 1-cent sales tax for 72 months, >= $900M (incl. $70M MAPS 4); Thunder $50M (~5.5%); 25-yr license (June 2025) with > $1B exit penalties
rows.label: c
rows.notes: Not an owner/league threat by the stated rule; sensitivity moves it into the threat group.

rows.owners: Peter J. Holt / Julianna Hawn Holt (Spurs Sports & Entertainment)
rows.said_or_done: May 2022 request to play more home games outside San Antonio (Austin) raised move fears; Holt letter: "I want to reassure you that the Spurs are in San Antonio to stay." Lease ends 2032; no owner relocation statement found.
rows.money_after: Bexar County Prop B 2025-11-04 (52.14%): venue tax up to $311M; city up to $489M in non-binding term sheet (2025-08-21, 7-4); Spurs >= $500M + overruns; July 2026 county allowed up to 4 home games/season elsewhere
rows.mechanism: County venue tax (voted); city funds (not voted)
rows.vote: Prop B 52.14%; Spurs-funded PAC $9.2M vs ~ $270K opposition
rows.label: c
rows.notes: Ambiguous (Austin games) but no owner threat by the stated rule.

rows.said_or_done: None documented.
rows.money_after: Bexar County $85M of $101.5M AT&T Center renovation (development agreement approved by Commissioners Court 2015-04-21); lease to 2032 with break fees up to $124M
rows.label: b/c
rows.notes: The ledger earlier dated the approval 2014-12-09, a date not found in the cited sources; corrected to the county release (Oct. 17, 2026).

rows.said_or_done: None documented.
rows.money_after: Target Center renovation: city $74M of ~$140M (final approval Mar 2016); team ~$58M; AEG ~$6M
rows.mechanism: City sales taxes redirected under 2012 Vikings stadium law
rows.label: b
rows.notes: Approval day approximate (March 2016).

rows.said_or_done: None documented.
rows.money_after: Philips (State Farm) Arena renovation: city $142.5M ($110M rental-car tax extension + $12.5M Turner Field sale + $20M property sales) of $192.5M; Hawks $50M; non-relocation to 2046, up to $200M break fee
rows.label: c
rows.notes: Approval day approximate.

rows.said_or_done: No relocation threat documented. After petitions for a referendum, the team withdrew from the deal (2017-08-28/29, citing costs and delays) and revived it when Greater Cleveland Congregations withdrew petitions (2017-08-31).
rows.money_after: "Q Transformation": public ~$70M principal of $140M (>= $160M with interest, Axios); lease extended to 2034; plus $40.5M (2019) county sin-tax bonds for repairs
rows.mechanism: County bonds, city admissions tax, Destination Cleveland
rows.vote: County & City councils (2017); referendum petitions withdrawn
rows.label: c
rows.notes: Approval day approximate.

rows.said_or_done: None documented (lease expiring 2019).
rows.money_after: CIB (Apr 2019): $360M renovation, state+CIB $270M + city $25M (= $295M public), Pacers $65M; plus ~$12.5M+/yr CIB operating reimbursements 2019-44; Pacers owe up to $750M if they leave
rows.label: b/c

rows.owners: Michael Jordan (seller 2023) -> Gabe Plotkin & Rick Schnall
rows.said_or_done: None documented. Lease required the city to keep the arena "among the most modern in the league" (WFAE paraphrase); city consultant said $173M was already contractually owed.
rows.money_after: 2022-06-13 (10-1): $215M arena renovation + $60M practice facility = $275M (tourism taxes); lease extended 2030 -> 2045. 2023 sale: no relocation talk found
rows.label: c
rows.notes: Team share not found -> public share n/a.

rows.said_or_done: None documented for the Jazz (district deal paired with the NHL team relocated from Arizona).
rows.money_after: Utah SB 272 (2024) + Salt Lake City 0.5% sales tax: ~$900M over 30 yrs ($525M Delta Center, $375M district); referendum drive dropped 2024-10-04
rows.label: c
rows.notes: Arena privately owned -> public share n/a.

rows.said_or_done: None documented.
rows.money_after: $226M Orange County tourist-tax package for Kia Center (Nov 2024); Magic $0
rows.label: c

rows.said_or_done: None documented.
rows.money_after: $180M Toyota Center overhaul with ~$95M State of Texas grant (Apr 2026)
rows.label: c

rows.said_or_done: None documented; lease ends 2029.
rows.money_after: 2024 state money for FedExForum (~$230M of $350M with Liberty Bowl) toward ~$550M plan; long-term lease still unsigned (Daily Memphian)
rows.label: c
rows.notes: Pending - excluded.

rows.owners: Miriam Adelson & Dumont family (majority, Dec 2023); Mark Cuban (minority)
rows.said_or_done: Owners pushed Texas casino legalization (2025 session); Patrick Dumont said a casino is not part of the arena plans; club "made it clear" it wants to stay in Dallas; preliminary deal (June 2026) for a site ~10 miles north of downtown; AAC lease runs to July 2031.
rows.money_after: None approved as of Oct 2026
rows.label: c
rows.notes: Not counted as an implied threat: the Dec 2023 sale went to the Las Vegas Sands owners (Adelson and Dumont families), but the buyers said they would "build on the team's success and legacy in Dallas" and had "no interest in moving the team to Vegas or out of North Texas" (FOX 4 via Fox 5 NY), and Cuban said the team would remain in Dallas; the out-of-town-buyer prong covers sales with no commitment to stay.

rows.owners: Bruce Ratner (bought 2004) -> Mikhail Prokhorov -> Joe Tsai
rows.said_or_done: Team sold (2004) to a developer whose plan was to move it to a new arena in Brooklyn (Atlantic Yards); played in Newark 2010-12, opened Barclays Center 2012-09-21.
rows.money_after: Destination (NY): IBO (2009) present-value subsidies: NYC $350M and State/MTA $142M incl. tax breaks; federal $194M via tax-exempt PILOT bonds; city net loss $40M (cash) or $180M incl. tax breaks; below-market land worth $50M-$114M excluded
rows.mechanism: Triple-tax-exempt PILOT bonds via Brooklyn Arena LDC; city/state capital; MTA land sale; tax exemptions
rows.label: c (IBO via Field of Schemes) + b (IBO 2023 structure)
rows.notes: Dates for sale agreement and state approval are approximate (not verified here); lag not used.

rows.said_or_done: Moved from Oakland to privately financed Chase Center (San Francisco); no request for public construction money documented.
rows.money_after: None for construction; Oakland/Alameda pursued Warriors for remaining 1996 renovation debt (see left_behind)
rows.label: c

rows.said_or_done: Moved from Crypto.com Arena to privately financed Intuit Dome in Inglewood; bought The Forum from MSG for $400M (2020) to end litigation.
rows.money_after: No public construction money identified
rows.label: c

rows.said_or_done: Detroit induced a move from (private) Palace of Auburn Hills to Little Caesars Arena; DDA notes describe bonds issued "to incentivize the Detroit Pistons to relocate to the City of Detroit."
rows.money_after: Detroit City Council 2017-06-20 approved $34.5M public funding for the Pistons move (Downtown Development Authority bonds); LCA overall public share est. 58% at 2013 plan
rows.label: b/c
rows.notes: Destination-type money; excluded from T vs N.

rows.said_or_done: No relocation threat documented. 2014: moved practice facility/offices to Camden NJ for a 10-yr $82M Grow NJ tax credit (EDA unanimous, June 2014). 2022-25: proposed privately financed 76 Place (approved by City Council), abandoned Jan 2025 for a joint South Philadelphia arena with Comcast Spectacor (~2031).
rows.money_after: NJ $82M tax credit (practice facility; 250-job minimum)
rows.label: c
rows.notes: Not an arena; excluded from comparison. The 2024 Camden arena talks are episode E51.

rows.label: c

rows.said_or_done: Crypto.com Arena privately financed by AEG (1999). No threat found.
rows.label: c

rows.said_or_done: United Center privately built by Reinsdorf/Wirtz JV (1994); annual property-tax appeals (prior round). No threat found.

rows.label: c

rows.said_or_done: Talks with another city: the Warriors and San Jose "have all but completed negotiations" on a $43M package including a $35M relocation fee, while the team sought a publicly financed Oakland arena (Sports Business Daily, Oct 19 1995, citing the San Francisco Chronicle).
rows.money_after: Oakland and Alameda County financed a renovation of the Coliseum arena: Memorandum of Understanding Feb 21 1996 (city and county to issue bonds); License Agreement July 1996, 20-year term 1997-2017 with four five-year options and renovation debt owed to 2027 if the team leaves early; the Coliseum Authority issued "$140 million to be repaid over 30 years" in August 1996 (Court of Appeal, A157688, 2020). Renovation cost $121M (left_behind.csv, c).
rows.mechanism: Coliseum Authority bonds repaid by the city and county (lease-revenue type per Bond Buyer, c)
rows.outcome: stayed (moved to San Francisco in 2019; arbitration and the courts held it to the renovation debt, see left_behind)
rows.label: c (threat) + b (court record of the deal)
rows.notes: Added Oct 18 2026 (missed in earlier rounds). The day of the August 1996 bond issue is not given (15th used); not in the capital comparison, whose deal list starts with the current arenas.

rows.said_or_done: Talks with another city: "Discussions between top state officials and leaders from Harris Blitzer Sports & Entertainment" about a Camden arena had run for about two months (ROI-NJ, July 18 2024, four anonymous sources); the team did not deny them ("We remain focused on bringing a state-of-the-art arena to Philadelphia, as we have been for the last four years"). Inquirer column (Jan 16 2025, one anonymous source): the Sixers kept negotiating with Camden after the downtown arena passed Council, and "Camden 'always' remained on the table".
rows.money_after: None in Philadelphia: the teams call the joint South Philadelphia arena with Comcast Spectacor privately funded, and Gov. Shapiro said the state would provide no money for new arenas (AP, June 22 2025). New Jersey's offer, not used: up to $400M of Aspire tax credits (ROI-NJ) or about $800M (Inquirer)
rows.outcome: stayed (no public money in Philadelphia to date)
rows.label: c (anonymous sources; the team did not confirm)
rows.notes: Split from E40 (the 2014 practice facility) on Oct 22 2026. Implied by the ledger rule ("talks with another city"). No 2024-25 board agenda or minutes of the New Jersey Economic Development Authority mentions the team (45 of 49 files read). Dated from the first report; the talks began about May 2024.

method: select t.id, t.team, t.owners, t.period, t.threat_class, t.said_or_done, t.alt_city, t.league_role, t.money_after, t.money_usd_m, t.mechanism, t.vote, t.threat_date, t.approval_date, t.approval_date_final, t.months_threat_to_approval, t.outcome, t.label, t.notes, t.id in (select id from comparison_ids where k = 'same_city_money') as same_city_money, t.id in (select id from comparison_ids where k = 'team_left') as team_left, t.id in (select id from comparison_ids where k = 'no_new_money') as no_new_money, (select months from threat_lags l where l.id = t.id) as lag_months, coalesce((select list(s.source_id order by s.ord) from threat_sources s where s.id = t.id), []) as sources from threats t order by t.id
